questions.question: What is the advantage of internal fertilisation?
options: A greater number of offspring are produced, ensuring species survival
It can take place in aquatic environments
Less care needs to be provided for gametes and offspring
There is less risk of the gametes drying out
questions.answer: **D.** Gametes stay inside the moist female reproductive tract.

questions.question: A section of DNA was found to have 40 cytosine bases and 50 thymine bases. What is the total number of deoxyribose sugar molecules in this sample?
questions.answer: **D.** G = C = 40 and A = T = 50, giving 180 nucleotides, each with one deoxyribose.

questions.question: The diagram shows how influenza is transmitted. Which situation would **least** likely result in transmission of the flu virus from one person to another?
options: A fly landing on an infected person, then on an uninfected person
Drinking from an unwashed cup previously used by an infected person
Being in the same room as someone showing flu symptoms
Eating food prepared by an infected person
questions.answer: **A.** Influenza is not normally vector-borne.

questions.question: Yeast reproduces asexually as shown. The offspring produced from this type of reproduction usually have:
options: half the number of chromosomes of their parents
genetic information identical to their parents
greater variation in characteristics than their parents
fewer organelles than their parents due to division
questions.answer: **B.** Budding follows mitosis, so offspring are clones.

questions.question: Genetically modified tomatoes contain a new substance with health benefits that turns them purple. What is inserted into the DNA of another plant to make it transgenic?
options: A gene from another species
A different gene from the same species
Chromosomes from the same species
Proteins from another species
questions.answer: **A.** A transgenic organism carries a gene from a different species.

questions.question: A section of DNA from a plant is shown. How many codons are shown in this section of DNA?
questions.answer: **B.** 12 base pairs give 12 bases on the coding strand, i.e. four triplets.

questions.question: Many bacteria and viruses can enter mucosal surfaces. When this occurs, they encounter features of adaptive immunity, including:
options: antihistamines
B lymphocytes
lysozymes
macrophages
questions.answer: **B.** B lymphocytes are part of adaptive immunity.

questions.question: Chagas disease is caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*, a protozoan with a flattened body and a flagellum, transmitted by triatomine ('kissing') bugs. It lives in human blood and reproduces by splitting in two. It is reasonable to conclude that *T. cruzi*:
options: has a digestive system
has a thick cell wall to resist macrophages
uses its flagellum for locomotion
is likely to be attached to the walls of the intestines
questions.answer: **C.** A flagellum is a locomotory structure suited to moving in blood.

questions.question: When is genetic drift most likely to be observed?
options: When environmental pressures select for favourable traits
When many mutations occur in the population
When there is allele flow from one population to another
When particular alleles disappear by chance as individuals die or do not reproduce
questions.answer: **D.** Drift is random change in allele frequencies.

questions.question: Which is evidence that a plant has an infectious disease?
options: Nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria on its roots
The plant is dark green and stunted due to phosphorus deficiency
Fungal hyphae growing out of its stomata
Wilting and drying out of root hairs during drought
questions.answer: **C.** Hyphae indicate a fungal pathogen.

questions.question: The pedigree shows the inheritance of a syndrome causing abnormally long, slender fingers and toes (shaded individuals are affected). Based on this pedigree, what is the mode of inheritance?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive
questions.answer: **B.** Unaffected parents have affected children (recessive), including an affected daughter with an unaffected father (autosomal). *Note: the paper calls this Marfan syndrome, which in reality is autosomal dominant.*

questions.question: The table shows six common chromosomal syndromes. Which of the following is correct? (Syndrome; number of chromosomes in genome; chromosome affected)
options: Down; 47; autosome
Edwards; 36; autosome
Klinefelter; 23; sex chromosome
Patau; 47; sex chromosome
questions.answer: **A.** Down syndrome is trisomy of autosome 21, giving 47 chromosomes.

questions.question: Which statement about melanoma is true?
options: Damage to the DNA of a cell is easier to cure than to prevent
Individuals born with a genetic predisposition will develop it at the same stage of life
There is a strong correlation between melanoma incidence, age and where you live
Whenever the DNA of a cell is damaged, melanoma will develop
questions.answer: **C.** Incidence rises with age and with UV exposure, which depends on location.

questions.question: Tetanus is caused by *Clostridium tetani*, a bacterium living in soil, dust and manure that enters through open wounds and produces a toxin. Which of the following is the best strategy for controlling the incidence of tetanus?
options: Antibiotics
Quarantine
Social distancing by two arm lengths
Washing hands with soap for 30 seconds
questions.answer: **A.** Tetanus is not passed between people; of these options only antibiotics act on the bacterium. *Note: in practice, vaccination and wound care are the main controls.*

questions.question: An inactivated polio vaccine given by injection has replaced the oral vaccine in Australia. Why are vaccinated individuals protected against polio?
options: The viruses in the vaccine are too weak to cause illness
The vaccine produces an inflammatory response
The viruses in the vaccine prevent further viral invasion
The vaccine stimulates the production of memory cells
questions.answer: **D.** Memory cells give a rapid secondary response.

questions.question: Which set of mechanisms do mammals use in response to a **decrease** in body temperature?
options: Vasodilation, contraction of hair erector muscles, sweating
Vasoconstriction, contraction of hair erector muscles, sweating
Vasoconstriction, contraction of hair erector muscles, shivering
Vasodilation, relaxation of hair erector muscles, shivering
questions.answer: **C.** All three conserve or generate heat.

questions.question: Pasteur boiled nutrient broth in flasks with S-shaped necks to test for spontaneous generation. Why did he use a swan-necked flask?
options: It allowed him to easily observe his results
The curved neck trapped airborne microbes and stopped them contaminating the broth
The glass was easy to sterilise, ensuring better microbial growth
The curved neck made the broth condense there, maximising exposure
questions.answer: **B.** Air could enter but microbes settled in the bend.

questions.question: The diagram shows negative feedback control of body temperature. What does the part labelled X represent?
options: Hypothalamus
Pituitary
Brain
Skin
questions.answer: **A.** The hypothalamus is the temperature control centre.

questions.question: The graph shows the number of new cases of the most common cancers diagnosed in Australia in 2019. What does this data represent?
options: Incidence
Morbidity rates
Mortality rates
Prevalence
questions.answer: **A.** Incidence is the number of new cases in a period.

questions.question: A highly contagious viral disease of birds (Newcastle disease), potentially causing up to 100% mortality, broke out in commercial poultry flocks near Sydney. It poses little public health risk. Which is the most effective control measure to prevent spread to other farms and native birds?
options: Destroying all poultry and restocking with unaffected birds
Vaccinating farmers and laboratory workers and monitoring affected birds
Quarantining farmers and laboratory workers and disinfecting affected properties
Quarantine, destruction of poultry and disinfection of affected properties
questions.answer: **D.** It removes the reservoir and blocks all routes of spread.

questions.question: The images show plant cells undergoing meiosis. The order of the first three stages is 4-2-3. Give the correct order of the last four stages.

Compare mitosis and meiosis by completing the missing entries:

| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Genetically | identical daughter cells | genetically different daughter cells |
| Type of cells produced | somatic | ? |
| Number of cell divisions | ? | ? |
| Number of daughter cells | ? | 4 |
questions.answer:
| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Type of cells produced | somatic | gametes |
| Number of cell divisions | 1 | 2 |
| Number of daughter cells | 2 | 4 |

questions.question:
The diagram shows exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes between prophase I and metaphase I of meiosis.

Identify this process.
questions.answer: **Crossing over** (recombination).

questions.question:
The diagram shows exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes between prophase I and metaphase I of meiosis.

Draw the resulting allele combinations on the chromatids.
questions.answer: The four chromatids carry: **Ab** (parental), **AB** (recombinant), **ab** (recombinant) and **aB** (parental).

questions.question: The Rhesus-positive allele is dominant. A mother with Rhesus-negative blood, whose husband is heterozygous, gives birth to a Rhesus-positive baby. What is the probability that a sibling will be born Rhesus negative? Show working.
questions.answer:
Mother $rr$, father $Rr$.

| | $r$ | $r$ |
|---|---|---|
| $R$ | $Rr$ | $Rr$ |
| $r$ | $rr$ | $rr$ |

Probability of an Rh-negative child $=\tfrac12$ (50%), independent of earlier children.

questions.question: A Rhesus-negative woman can make antibodies against the blood of a Rhesus-positive foetus. Give a possible explanation for why subsequent pregnancies could trigger an immune response.
questions.answer: In the first Rh-positive pregnancy (usually at birth), foetal red cells can enter her blood. The Rh antigen is foreign, so she produces antibodies and memory cells. In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, the secondary response rapidly produces large amounts of antibody that can cross the placenta and attack the foetus's red blood cells.

questions.question: The spinifex hopping mouse is a small desert-dwelling mammal (an endotherm). Outline one physiological and one behavioural adaptation it may have.
questions.answer:
**Physiological:** its kidneys produce very concentrated urine, conserving water.

**Behavioural:** it is nocturnal and shelters in humid burrows by day, avoiding heat and water loss.

*Note: the paper calls it a marsupial; it is actually a rodent (placental mammal).*

questions.question: Outline two mechanisms in plants that allow water balance to be maintained in an arid environment, and explain how each does so.
questions.answer:
| Mechanism | How water balance is maintained |
|---|---|
| Sunken stomata | Stomata in pits trap humid air, reducing the diffusion gradient and so transpiration |
| Thick waxy cuticle | A waterproof layer reduces evaporation from the leaf surface |

Others include reduced or rolled leaves, closing stomata in heat, and water storage tissue.

questions.question: Scientists often study the effects of environment on phenotype by studying identical twins. Discuss this statement using examples of the effect of environment on phenotype.
questions.answer:
Identical twins have the same genotype, so differences between them can be attributed to environment, particularly in twins raised apart. For example, height is polygenic but is limited by poor nutrition; skin colour darkens with UV exposure; body mass depends on diet and exercise. Outside humans, the Arctic hare's coat changes with season.

However, twin studies have limits: twins often share much of their environment, pairs raised apart are rare (small samples), and epigenetic changes or new mutations mean they are not perfectly identical. Phenotype results from genes and environment interacting.

questions.question:
Malaria is caused by parasites transmitted by female *Anopheles* mosquitoes. In 2018 there were about 228 million cases and 405 000 deaths.

Use the map to describe the global death rate from malaria in 2017.
questions.answer: Death rates are highest in sub-Saharan (central and western) Africa, in places exceeding 100 per 100 000; lower rates occur in parts of South and South-East Asia and Oceania; Europe, North America, Australia and most other regions have very few deaths (0–2.5 per 100 000).

questions.question:
Malaria is caused by parasites transmitted by female *Anopheles* mosquitoes. In 2018 there were about 228 million cases and 405 000 deaths.

Suggest why deaths are concentrated near the equator.
questions.answer: The warm, humid tropical climate suits breeding of the *Anopheles* vector and development of the *Plasmodium* parasite (and many of these regions have limited health resources).

questions.question:
Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutated allele (HbS) of the haemoglobin gene: the codon GAG becomes GUG (in mRNA), so valine replaces glutamic acid. People with two HbS alleles have the disease; carriers have some protection against malaria.

What type of mutation is this?
questions.answer: A **point mutation** (base substitution, causing a missense change).

questions.question:
Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutated allele (HbS) of the haemoglobin gene: the codon GAG becomes GUG (in mRNA), so valine replaces glutamic acid. People with two HbS alleles have the disease; carriers have some protection against malaria.

Two parents heterozygous for the sickle cell allele have a child. What is the probability that the child is a carrier, with a protective advantage against malaria but without sickle cell anaemia? Show working.
questions.answer:
Cross HbA HbS × HbA HbS gives HbA HbA : HbA HbS : HbS HbS $=1:2:1$.
So the probability of a carrier is $\tfrac12$ (50%).

*Note: the original asks for the probability the child "will not develop malaria"; carriers are only partly protected, so the question has been reworded.*

questions.question: In which region of DNA do single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) more commonly occur?
questions.answer: In **non-coding** regions of DNA.

questions.question:
Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutated allele (HbS) of the haemoglobin gene: the codon GAG becomes GUG (in mRNA), so valine replaces glutamic acid. People with two HbS alleles have the disease; carriers have some protection against malaria.

Referring to the world HbS allele frequency map, explain how allele frequencies for SNPs could be used to determine the origin of a particular allele.
questions.answer:
By sampling many populations and mapping the frequency of the allele, patterns of origin and spread can be inferred: an allele is often most frequent, and its surrounding DNA most varied, where it arose long ago, with frequency declining along migration routes.

The map shows the highest HbS frequencies (up to about 18%) in central and western Africa, lower values in the Middle East and India, and near zero elsewhere. This suggests an African origin with spread by migration, maintained where malaria is common because carriers have a survival advantage. Selection also affects frequency, so haplotype (linked SNP) analysis is needed to confirm origin.

questions.question: Using an example, outline the steps involved in gene cloning.
questions.answer:
Example: human insulin.

1. Cut out the insulin gene (or make it from mRNA) and cut a bacterial plasmid with the same restriction enzyme.
2. Join gene and plasmid with DNA ligase.
3. Insert the recombinant plasmid into *E. coli*.
4. Select and culture the transformed bacteria; as they divide, the gene is copied (and insulin can be produced).

questions.question: Evaluate the effect of mutation, gene flow and genetic drift on the gene pool of populations.
questions.answer:
- **Mutation** is the only source of new alleles. Its effect per generation is small (most mutations are neutral or harmful), but over long periods it is essential for variation.
- **Gene flow** (migration) moves alleles between populations: it can quickly add or remove alleles, especially in small populations, and makes populations more alike.
- **Genetic drift** is random change in allele frequency (e.g. bottleneck or founder effects). It can eliminate or fix alleles and strongly reduce variation, mainly in small populations.

**Judgement:** all three change gene pools; mutation matters most for creating variation in the long term, while drift and gene flow can have much larger immediate effects, depending on population size.

questions.question: For a named cancer, describe the cause and effects of the disease.
questions.answer:
**Melanoma** (skin cancer).

**Cause:** UV radiation damages DNA in melanocytes; mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle (proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes) lead to uncontrolled division. Risk is increased by sunburn (especially in childhood), fair skin and family history.

**Effects:** a new or changing mole (asymmetry, irregular border, varied colour), which may itch or bleed. The tumour invades deeper tissue and can metastasise through lymph and blood to organs such as lungs, liver and brain, disrupting their function and possibly causing death. Treatment (surgery, immunotherapy) also affects quality of life.

questions.question:
Pertussis (whooping cough) is a bacterial infection caused by *Bordetella pertussis*. The diagram shows an immune response to it.

Identify cell X.
questions.answer: A **helper T cell**.

questions.question:
Pertussis (whooping cough) is a bacterial infection caused by *Bordetella pertussis*. The diagram shows an immune response to it.

Describe the role of memory B cells.
questions.answer: Memory B cells remain in the body long after the infection. On re-exposure to the same antigen they recognise it and rapidly divide and differentiate into plasma cells, producing large amounts of specific antibody quickly (secondary response), often preventing symptoms.

questions.question: Parents of infants in intensive care are asked to have a pertussis booster vaccine. Their immune response is shown. Explain the shape of the graph.
questions.answer: At first exposure there is a lag while B and T cells with matching receptors are selected and clone, then a small, slow primary peak that declines as antibodies are broken down and plasma cells die. Memory cells remain, so at the secondary exposure antibody rises much faster, to a much higher peak, and stays elevated for longer.

questions.question:
New cases of whooping cough in a region of Australia, 2017:

| Month | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cases | 22 | 65 | 64 | 103 | 120 | 126 | 160 | 104 | 81 |

Graph the data.
questions.answer: Month (independent variable) on the horizontal axis and number of new cases on the vertical axis, with an even scale, labels, title and accurately plotted points joined.

questions.question:
New cases of whooping cough in a region of Australia, 2017:

| Month | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cases | 22 | 65 | 64 | 103 | 120 | 126 | 160 | 104 | 81 |

Identify a trend in the data.
questions.answer: New cases generally increase from April to a peak of 160 in October, then decline in November and December.

questions.question: As Chief Medical Officer of a European country you face an outbreak of Marburg virus: a haemorrhagic fever with a fatality ratio of up to 88%, spread to humans by fruit bats, then person to person by direct contact with bodily fluids and contaminated surfaces and materials; incubation 2–21 days. Outline and explain procedures that could be used to prevent the spread of the disease.
questions.answer:
- **Identify and isolate cases:** rapid testing; isolate patients in specialised units, breaking contact transmission.
- **Contact tracing and quarantine** of contacts for at least 21 days, the maximum incubation period.
- **Protective equipment** (gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection) and training for health workers and carers, as the virus enters through mucous membranes and broken skin.
- **Hygiene:** handwashing; disinfect surfaces; incinerate or sterilise contaminated bedding and clothing.
- **Safe burials**, avoiding contact with bodies.
- **Travel and border measures:** screening and restrictions for affected areas.
- **Reduce animal contact:** avoid bats, caves and mines where they roost.
- **Public education** with clear, honest information about symptoms and what to do, to gain cooperation.
- Support **vaccine and antiviral trials**, offering candidates to contacts and health workers.

questions.question:
The diagram outlines events in the production of a polypeptide chain in a eukaryotic cell.

Name the process at step 1.
questions.answer: **Transcription.**

questions.question:
The diagram outlines events in the production of a polypeptide chain in a eukaryotic cell.

Name the product of step 1.
questions.answer: **mRNA** (initially pre-mRNA, which is processed in step 2).

questions.question:
The diagram outlines events in the production of a polypeptide chain in a eukaryotic cell.

Describe what is happening at step 4.
questions.answer: **Translation:** the ribosome moves along the mRNA; tRNA molecules with anticodons complementary to each codon deliver specific amino acids, which are joined by peptide bonds to form a growing polypeptide chain.

questions.question: Biotechnology has affected Earth's biodiversity for many years. Outline one example of biotechnology from the past, one from the present and one potential future example. Evaluate their effects on biodiversity.
questions.answer:
**Past: selective breeding.** Farmers bred from plants and animals with desired traits (e.g. wheat, cattle). This narrowed gene pools and replaced many local varieties, and farming expansion destroyed habitat. Overall it reduced genetic diversity, though it also produced new breeds.

**Present: transgenic crops**, e.g. Bt cotton. Large monocultures of very similar plants reduce genetic diversity and increase vulnerability to disease; pests may evolve resistance. However, less insecticide spraying can benefit non-target insects.

**Future: CRISPR-edited climate-tolerant crops** (or gene drives against pests). They could reduce the need to clear more land, and edits can restore variation, but wide planting of a few elite lines would further narrow gene pools, and gene drives could eliminate a species with unpredictable ecological effects.

**Evaluation:** biotechnology has mostly reduced genetic diversity in agriculture, mainly through uniformity. The impact depends on management: seed banks, crop rotation, refuges and regulation can limit the loss.

questions.question: In one calendar year, a population (aged 16 and over) of 6.1 million had 192 760 total cases of diabetes, of which 29 280 were new. Calculate the prevalence of diabetes.
questions.answer:
Prevalence uses all existing cases:
$$\frac{192\,760}{6.1\times10^6}\times100=3.16\%\quad(\approx3160\text{ per }100\,000).$$

questions.question:
Type 1 diabetes occurs when the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas (genes and environmental factors such as viruses are thought to trigger it). Type 2 is largely the result of lifestyle factors. Graph 1 shows prevalence by age in Australia, Graph 2 incidence of type 1, and Graph 3 age-standardised prevalence of type 2 in men in 1980 and 2014.

Using the data, identify trends for type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
questions.answer:
**Type 1:** prevalence in Graph 1 is highest at 10–19 years (about 26 per 100 000) and falls steadily with age (about 2 at 70+). Incidence (Graph 2) has risen over time in all four places, e.g. Finland from about 11 (1950) to about 62 per 100 000 per year (2007), with large differences between countries.

**Type 2:** (insulin-treated) prevalence is near zero in childhood and rises with age to a peak at 70–79 (about 280 per 100 000), roughly ten times the type 1 peak. Between 1980 and 2014 prevalence in men increased in most countries, especially in the Middle East, North Africa and parts of Asia and the Pacific.

*Note: the school provided no marking guide for Question 32; these answers are worked from the data.*

questions.question:
Type 1 diabetes occurs when the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas (genes and environmental factors such as viruses are thought to trigger it). Type 2 is largely the result of lifestyle factors. Graph 1 shows prevalence by age in Australia, Graph 2 incidence of type 1, and Graph 3 age-standardised prevalence of type 2 in men in 1980 and 2014.

Analyse factors that could account for the trends in type 1 and type 2 diabetes, supporting your answer with reference to the data.
questions.answer:
**Type 1** (autoimmune)

- Onset mostly in childhood and adolescence explains the peak at 10–19 (Graph 1); lower prevalence at older ages reflects fewer new cases then, earlier generations having had lower incidence and reduced life expectancy.
- The rapid rise since 1950 (Graph 2) is too fast for changes in gene frequency alone, so environmental triggers are likely: viral infections, less early-life microbial exposure, early diet, low vitamin D. Better diagnosis and recording also contribute.
- Differences between countries (Finland highest, Germany low) suggest both genetic susceptibility and environment (e.g. latitude and sunlight).

**Type 2** (insulin resistance)

- Prevalence rises with age as insulin sensitivity declines and effects of lifestyle accumulate; the fall at 80+ may reflect earlier death of people with diabetes.
- The global increase from 1980 to 2014 (Graph 3) corresponds with urbanisation, energy-dense diets, physical inactivity and obesity.
- Regional differences reflect rates of these changes and genetic susceptibility in some populations.
- Longer life expectancy and better survival and screening raise prevalence.

**Limitations:** the maps show correlation only, Graph 1 counts only insulin-treated type 2 cases (underestimating it) and comes from one country, so cause cannot be established from these data alone.
